rv.q: Richard Eyre's fluent production tells the story of Ward's downfall with a bracing mixture of humour and indignation.
This is a powerful musical not about revolution but about defeat and decay and it is well worth seeing.
Ward remains oddly detached from his own life, until he detaches himself by suicide during the climactic trial, which crowns the second half.
But, much as I admire the musical's good intentions and professional skill, Lloyd Webber's instinctive romanticism sits oddly with a social and political critique.
Lloyd Webber's music is pleasing, though it doesn't do much to evoke the pop culture of the period.
Yet the show proves a strangely tepid affair.
This lurid tale of a well-dressed, ax-wielding stockbroker in late-20th-century Manhattan is often a hoot, if not quite the unsettling “musical thriller” it’s been advertised as.
It's a story that offered so much but as a show Stephen Ward returns so little.
But for the moment it looks like a very honourable failure.

The Cold War was at its height, provoking fears that British military secrets had been leaked during pillow talk, although Ward, in one ofthe show's many grubby lines, describes this as unlikely since Christine usually had her mouth full. Lloyd Webber has stated his wish to rehabilitate Ward, whom he views as an Establishment scapegoat.
Who this boring, mildly melodious, odious show is meant for is a mystery.
In the event, I faced the music - and the show - and it is, as I had feared, the biggest Christmas turkey in town.

cn.t: Lloyd Webber's Profumo affair musical divides critics: some praise its ambitious subject and slick production, but many find it misconceived and dramatically inert, with the composer's romanticism clashing with political critique.
